script.opening: "My right heel’s been killing me for a few weeks. The worst bit is the first few steps when I get out of bed — it’s like stepping on a stone or a knife — then it eases off as I get going, but comes back after I’ve been sitting. I’ve started running and I’m on my feet all day. What is it?"

facts.text: About 6 weeks, right heel. Underneath, towards the inside of the heel — points to it on camera and says it’s tender when he presses there. First steps in the morning are the worst; eases after 10 minutes; back after sitting and at the end of a shift.
Took up running 2 months ago "to lose a bit of weight" — went from nothing to 5 km four times a week. Old trainers. No single injury moment.

Can walk on it; not limping badly. No pain at night or at rest. No swelling, no bruising. No tingling or numbness in the foot. No back pain. No other joints painful, no morning stiffness elsewhere, no eye problems, no bowel problems. No pain squeezing the sides of the heel.
BMI about 32 — put on 2 stone in the last 3 years. No diabetes known. No medicines. Occasional ibuprofen. No asthma, no stomach problems. No allergies.
Warehouse supervisor — on his feet on concrete floors 10 hours a day in steel toe-cap boots. Married, two children. Non-smoker, drinks 15 units a week.

Easy-going, a bit frustrated. You don’t want to give up running now you’ve started. Ask: "Will it go?" If weight is raised sensitively, accept it ("the running was meant to help with that"); if raised bluntly, become a bit defensive.

ice.ideas: "I thought it was the running. Maybe a heel spur?"
ice.concerns: "I’m worried I’ll have to stop running, and how long it’ll last with my job."
ice.expectations: "Something to fix it — maybe an injection or an X-ray."

cues: "The first few steps when I get out of bed" — the classic pattern.
"I’ve started running and I’m on my feet all day" — load to modify.
"I don’t want to give up the running" — negotiate staying active.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PLANTAR FASCIITIS — "first-step" plantar heel pain (worst in the morning/after rest, easing with walking) with tenderness at the medial calcaneal plantar-fascia origin and typical risk factors
Confirms clinically (typical history + localised tenderness) and recognises imaging is not routinely required

Distinguishes it from calcaneal stress fracture (new load/point bony tenderness), tarsal tunnel/nerve entrapment, fat-pad atrophy, Achilles pathology and inflammatory/seronegative arthropathy (enthesitis — asks about other joints/back/psoriasis)

Manages conservatively — education, load modification keeping tolerable activity, calf and plantar-fascia stretching with strengthening, supportive footwear/low-cost heel cushioning, weight discussed sensitively, analgesia only if suitable (JOSPT/APTA 2023; BNF)

Knows escalation — review adherence and diagnosis, physiotherapy/podiatry, night splint, selective corticosteroid injection, specialist referral (shockwave only under NICE HTG200 special arrangements) for refractory cases — and sets realistic timeline expectations
Reassures about the favourable but slow (months) course, acknowledges the impact on work/running, and checks understanding of stretching/footwear advice
Engages the patient in load modification (and a sensitive conversation about weight) without being dismissive of his wish to stay active

Safety-nets and follows up: review if not improving, escalate if refractory, and red flags warranting reconsideration (point bony tenderness/stress fracture, neurological symptoms, systemic/inflammatory features) — conservative-first management

worked.txt: "This is plantar fasciitis — strain of the band of tissue along the sole, where it attaches to the heel bone. That classic ‘stepping on a stone’ pain on the first steps, easing as you move, is the giveaway. The new running and being on your feet all day have set it off."

"Just to be safe — was there a specific injury? And do you get any tingling or numbness in the foot? … (Waits for his answers.) I’d also like to examine the heel in person, to check whether the tenderness is along the fascia rather than a pinpoint on the bone, as that helps rule out a stress fracture."

"The mainstays are stretching and strengthening — your calf and the sole — which I’ll show you, supportive cushioned footwear or a cheap heel cup, and adjusting the running so you stay active without big jumps in distance. Painkillers can help you keep moving if they suit you. If you’d find it useful at some point, we can also talk about weight, as it’s one of the things that loads the heel."
"I’ll be honest — it can take a few months to fully settle, but it does get better with these measures, and most people don’t need anything more."

"If it’s stubborn, we’ll first check the plan and the diagnosis, then physiotherapy helps, a night splint can help the morning pain, and there are options like a steroid injection (used carefully) or specialist treatments such as shockwave therapy, which is only offered in special research-style arrangements because the evidence is uncertain."
"Come back if it’s not improving, if you get a sharp pinpoint pain on the heel bone (especially after upping your running), or any numbness or pins and needles — those would make me think again."

f.learning: PLANTAR FASCIITIS is the commonest cause of plantar heel pain, recognised by classic "FIRST-STEP" pain — worst on the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with walking, and returning after prolonged standing — with tenderness at the MEDIAL CALCANEAL tubercle (plantar-fascia origin); risk factors include overuse/new running, prolonged standing, higher body weight, unsupportive footwear and a tight calf/Achilles; chronic cases are often degenerative and load-related ("plantar fasciopathy"). Diagnosis is clinical (typical history plus localised tenderness, ± pain on dorsiflexing the toes) and imaging is not routinely required. Distinguish it from a calcaneal STRESS FRACTURE (recent increase in load/trauma, point bony tenderness, positive squeeze test), fat-pad atrophy (central heel, older), tarsal tunnel/nerve entrapment (burning/tingling/numbness), Achilles/insertional pathology, and inflammatory/seronegative arthropathy with enthesitis (ask about other joints, back pain, psoriasis, eye/GI symptoms). Manage conservatively — most improve, though recovery commonly takes several months (JOSPT/APTA 2023, international): education, load modification keeping up tolerable activity rather than complete rest, calf and plantar-fascia STRETCHING with progressive strengthening, supportive FOOTWEAR with optional low-cost heel cushioning, WEIGHT discussed sensitively (not a condition of treatment), and paracetamol or a short NSAID course only if suitable (BNF), which are first-line and effective for most. For persistent pain, review adherence and the diagnosis, then escalate to physiotherapy/podiatry, a night splint, a selective corticosteroid injection (risk of fat-pad atrophy/fascia rupture), and specialist referral (extracorporeal shockwave therapy only under NICE HTG200 special arrangements, as effectiveness is uncertain). Reassure about the favourable but slow course, set realistic timeline expectations, give stretching/footwear and load/weight advice, and safety-net for features that would prompt reconsideration (stress-fracture point tenderness, neurological symptoms, inflammatory/systemic features).

knowledge.summary: First-step plantar heel pain with tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle is plantar heel pain from plantar fasciopathy, a clinical diagnosis. Educate, adjust load without stopping activity, stretch the calf and plantar fascia, strengthen, use supportive footwear and a cheap heel cushion. Recovery often takes months. Reconsider the diagnosis for red flags, focal bony tenderness after a rise in running, nerve symptoms or inflammatory features. Injection and shockwave are not first-line.

points.t: Gradual medial plantar heel pain, worst on the first steps after rest and easing with activity, then worse with prolonged standing. Tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle; pain on passive toe dorsiflexion. Neurovascular examination normal. Imaging is not routine [1]. Chronic cases are often degenerative and load-related rather than purely inflammatory, so “plantar fasciopathy” is the more accurate term.

Calcaneal stress fracture (recent jump in running, focal bony pain, positive squeeze test), fat-pad syndrome (central heel), tarsal tunnel syndrome or S1 radiculopathy (burning, tingling, numbness; examine the nerves and back), insertional Achilles tendinopathy (posterior heel), and enthesitis in spondyloarthritis (inflammatory back pain, psoriasis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease) [3].

JOSPT/APTA [1]: education, plantar-fascia and calf stretching, progressive strengthening, and load modification. Keep up tolerable activity rather than resting completely, and avoid sudden rises in running or standing load. Supportive footwear; a low-cost prefabricated heel cup or insole can help comfort. Custom orthoses are not needed at first presentation.

Paracetamol or a short topical or oral NSAID course only if suitable for the patient, dose per BNF. Check renal, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal risk before an oral NSAID. Analgesia supports activity; it is not the treatment.
Higher body weight is a risk factor. Weight can be discussed sensitively as part of long-term load reduction, but it is not a condition of treatment.

Review adherence and the diagnosis first. Then physiotherapy or podiatry, a night splint for persistent first-step pain, and only then a selective corticosteroid injection (short-term relief; risks of fascia rupture and fat-pad atrophy; not repeated routinely). Shockwave therapy: NICE HTG200 [2] allows it only with special arrangements for governance, consent and audit because effectiveness is uncertain.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Weight raised sensitively; NSAID safety checked; physiotherapy, then selective injection or specialist options if persistent.
Red flags for fracture, infection and nerve problems; honest months-long timescale; review at about 6 weeks; teach-back.

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Idea (the running caused it), concern (stopping running; work), expectation (diagnosis and a fix).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

model.text: Hello Mr Denton, I’m Dr Hughes. What brings you in?

My right heel’s been killing me for a few weeks. The worst bit is the first few steps when I get out of bed. It’s like stepping on a stone or a knife. Then it eases off as I get going, but comes back after I’ve been sitting. I’ve started running and I’m on my feet all day. What is it?
That’s a very clear description, thank you. I’ll ask a few more questions and have a look, and then I’ll explain what I think it is.
Where exactly is the pain? Show me with a finger.
Underneath, towards the inside of the heel.
When did you start running, and how quickly did you build it up? Was there a moment it started, or a particular run?
model.why: Load change; screens for stress fracture

model.text: Only recently. I probably went at it a bit hard. No single moment, it just crept up.
Can you put your full weight on it? Is it ever painful at night, or constant even at rest?
model.why: Red flags: weight-bearing, night and rest pain

model.text: I can walk on it. It’s fine at night.
Any burning, tingling or numbness in the foot, or back pain going down the leg?
No, nothing like that.
Any back pain and stiffness that’s worse in the mornings, other painful or swollen joints, psoriasis, eye inflammation or bowel problems? And have you been well in yourself, no fevers or weight loss?
model.why: Inflammatory enthesitis and systemic red flags (NG65)

model.text: No. The only change in weight is that I’ve put some on, which is partly why I started running.
How is it affecting your work and life?
I’m on my feet all day, so by the end of the shift it’s sore again. I don’t want to give up the running now I’ve started.
Let me watch you walk and then examine both feet, including a quick check of the nerves.

You’re tender right here on the inside front of the heel bone, and bending your toes back brings on the pain. Squeezing the heel bone from the sides doesn’t hurt, so there’s no sign of a stress fracture. Your calf is tight. Pulses, feeling and reflexes are normal, and the Achilles is fine.
model.why: Medial tubercle tenderness, negative squeeze, tight calf, normal neurovascular

model.text: What did you think was going on? And what worries you most?
I thought it was the running. I’m worried I’ll have to stop, and how long it’ll last with my job.

You’re right that the running has played a part. This is plantar fasciitis: the tough band under your foot is strained where it attaches to the heel bone. Long days standing plus building up running quickly overloaded it. It explains that first-step pain exactly. We don’t need a scan.
model.why: Names diagnosis; links to load; no imaging

model.text: Will it go?
Most people get better, but I’ll be honest: it often takes several months, and it helps to know that from the start.

You don’t need to stop moving. Rest completely and it tends to stiffen; overload it and it flares. So cut the running back to a level that doesn’t make the next morning worse, perhaps swapping some for cycling or swimming, then build up gradually.
I can do that.

Stretch your calf and the sole of your foot every day, especially before those first steps in the morning, and I’ll show you some strengthening exercises. Supportive, cushioned shoes for work, and a cheap heel cup from a pharmacy is worth trying. Expensive custom insoles aren’t needed at this stage.
Paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory gel can take the edge off so you can keep moving. Any stomach, kidney or heart problems I should know about before tablets like ibuprofen?
model.why: Analgesia to support activity; NSAID safety

model.text: No, none.
You mentioned the weight. Carrying less does take load off the heel over time. If you’d like help with that, we can talk about it, but it’s not a condition of getting better.
model.why: Raises weight sensitively and offers, not imposes

model.text: Fair enough. The running was meant to help with that.
And it still can, once the heel settles. If it’s not improving after several weeks of this, I’ll refer you to physio. Injections and other treatments are for the minority who don’t settle.
model.why: Escalation pathway: physio, then selective options

model.text: Come back sooner if you can’t put weight on it, you get a sharp pinpoint pain in the heel bone itself, especially after a run, the heel becomes swollen, hot or red, or you get numbness or tingling in the foot, or pain at night. Can you tell me the plan so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Red flags: stress fracture, infection, nerve; teach-back

model.text: Keep moving but cut the running back, stretch every morning, better shoes and a heel cup, painkillers if I need them. Back if it’s no better in a few weeks or I get those warning signs.
That’s it. Let’s book a review in about six weeks.

social.t: Standing all day loads the heel. Supportive footwear and, where possible, breaks from standing help.
He started running to manage his weight. Keeping him active in some form protects that goal.

legal.t: Most people with plantar heel pain stay at work. If standing all day is not possible for a period, a fit note can advise altered duties or reduced standing rather than time off.

professional.t: Routine imaging and early injections add cost and risk without benefit in a typical case.
Explaining why rest is not the answer, and agreeing a running plan with him, supports adherence.

community.t: Many areas offer self-referral to MSK physiotherapy or podiatry for persistent symptoms.
Local weight-management or activity schemes can be offered if he wants help.

redFlags: Unable to weight-bear, focal bony tenderness or positive squeeze test after a rise in running: calcaneal stress fracture
Heel swelling, warmth, redness or fever: infection
Night or rest pain, weight loss, known malignancy: tumour
Burning, tingling, numbness or back pain: nerve entrapment or radiculopathy
Inflammatory back pain, psoriasis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease: enthesitis (NG65)
ice: Concern: having to stop running; coping at work
Expectation: a diagnosis and a fix

playbook.diagnosis: “This is plantar fasciitis: the band of tissue under your foot is overloaded where it joins the heel bone.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of a bowstring under your foot. Overnight it tightens up, so the first steps pull hard where it joins the heel. As you walk it loosens, which is why it eases. Too much load too quickly has frayed it where it’s anchored.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried you’d have to stop running. You don’t: we’ll adjust the load so the heel can recover and then build you back up.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him active and at work; offer weight support on his terms.
sharedPlan: Education and a realistic timescale of months
Daily calf and plantar-fascia stretching; progressive strengthening
Paracetamol or topical or short oral NSAID if suitable (BNF)
Physiotherapy if persistent; injection or shockwave (HTG200) only selectively
safetyNet: Unable to weight-bear or pinpoint bone pain: urgent review
Hot, swollen or red heel, or fever
Numbness, tingling, night pain; review at about 6 weeks

pitfalls.intro: A textbook story. Marks go to excluding a stress fracture and nerve causes, advising load change rather than rest, and handling his wish to keep running and the weight question well.

items.fail: Not considering a stress fracture after a rapid rise in running.
items.why: Focal bony pain and a positive squeeze test need imaging.
items.fix: Ask about the build-up and do the squeeze test.

items.why: The diagnosis is clinical; imaging is for atypical features.
Load modification with tolerable activity is recommended.

items.fail: Injection or shockwave at first presentation.
items.why: Not first-line; injection risks rupture and fat-pad atrophy; HTG200 requires special arrangements.
items.fix: Stretch, strengthen, footwear; physiotherapy if persistent.

items.why: He started running to address it; blame disengages him.
items.fix: Offer support and link it to his own goal.

items.why: Recovery often takes months; false hope reduces adherence.
items.fix: Give an honest timescale and a review date.

wordPics.fail: Orders an X-ray for a typical case; tells him to stop all activity; offers an injection or anti-inflammatories as the main treatment; misses the stress-fracture question after rapid running build-up; lectures on weight.
wordPics.pass: Recognises plantar fasciitis, examines for a stress fracture and nerve causes, gives stretching, load, footwear and analgesia advice, sets a realistic timescale and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: keeps him running at a tolerable load; explains the load mechanism in his terms; offers weight support without making it a condition; screens for inflammatory enthesitis; places injection and shockwave correctly as later, selective options; arranges review.

avoid.instead: “Cut back to a level that doesn’t make the next morning worse, then build up gradually.”
avoid.why: Complete rest is not recommended; load modification is.

avoid.dont: “You need to lose weight or it won’t get better.”
avoid.instead: “Carrying less takes load off the heel over time. We can help if you’d like.”
avoid.why: Weight is a risk factor, not a condition of treatment, and blaming loses engagement.

avoid.instead: “Most people get better with stretching and load changes. Injections are for the few who don’t.”
avoid.why: Injection is not first-line and carries risks of fascia rupture and fat-pad atrophy.

Calcaneal stress fracture (recent jump in running, focal bony pain, positive squeeze test), fat-pad syndrome (central heel), tarsal tunnel syndrome or S1 radiculopathy (burning, tingling, numbness; examine the nerves and back), insertional Achilles tendinopathy (posterior heel), and enthesitis in spondyloarthritis (inflammatory back pain, psoriasis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease) [3].

JOSPT/APTA [1]: education, plantar-fascia and calf stretching, progressive strengthening, and load modification. Keep up tolerable activity rather than resting completely, and avoid sudden rises in running or standing load. Supportive footwear; a low-cost prefabricated heel cup or insole can help comfort. Custom orthoses are not needed at first presentation.

Paracetamol or a short topical or oral NSAID course only if suitable for the patient, dose per BNF. Check renal, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal risk before an oral NSAID. Analgesia supports activity; it is not the treatment.
Higher body weight is a risk factor. Weight can be discussed sensitively as part of long-term load reduction, but it is not a condition of treatment.

Review adherence and the diagnosis first. Then physiotherapy or podiatry, a night splint for persistent first-step pain, and only then a selective corticosteroid injection (short-term relief; risks of fascia rupture and fat-pad atrophy; not repeated routinely). Shockwave therapy: NICE HTG200 [2] allows it only with special arrangements for governance, consent and audit because effectiveness is uncertain.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the classic first-step pain uninterrupted.
Standing job, new running, weight gain as his reason for running, and his wish to keep active.
Picked up the rapid build-up of running as a stress-fracture risk and his fear of having to stop.
Idea (the running caused it), concern (stopping running; work), expectation (diagnosis and a fix).
Gait, both feet, medial tubercle tenderness, calcaneal squeeze, calf tightness, neurovascular examination; no imaging.
Plantar fasciopathy versus stress fracture, fat pad, tarsal tunnel, S1 radiculopathy, Achilles and enthesitis.
Asked about weight-bearing, night and rest pain, nerve symptoms, inflammatory features and systemic symptoms.
Named plantar fasciitis and explained the load mechanism.
Load modification without complete rest; stretching and strengthening; footwear and heel cup; analgesia if suitable.
Weight raised sensitively; NSAID safety checked; physiotherapy, then selective injection or specialist options if persistent.
Red flags for fracture, infection and nerve problems; honest months-long timescale; review at about 6 weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Standing all day loads the heel. Supportive footwear and, where possible, breaks from standing help.
He started running to manage his weight. Keeping him active in some form protects that goal.

legal.t: Most people with plantar heel pain stay at work. If standing all day is not possible for a period, a fit note can advise altered duties or reduced standing rather than time off.

professional.t: Routine imaging and early injections add cost and risk without benefit in a typical case.
Explaining why rest is not the answer, and agreeing a running plan with him, supports adherence.

community.t: Many areas offer self-referral to MSK physiotherapy or podiatry for persistent symptoms.
Local weight-management or activity schemes can be offered if he wants help.

redFlags: Unable to weight-bear, focal bony tenderness or positive squeeze test after a rise in running: calcaneal stress fracture
Heel swelling, warmth, redness or fever: infection
Night or rest pain, weight loss, known malignancy: tumour
Burning, tingling, numbness or back pain: nerve entrapment or radiculopathy
Inflammatory back pain, psoriasis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease: enthesitis (NG65)
ice: Concern: having to stop running; coping at work
Expectation: a diagnosis and a fix

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is plantar fasciitis: the band of tissue under your foot is overloaded where it joins the heel bone.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a bowstring under your foot. Overnight it tightens up, so the first steps pull hard where it joins the heel. As you walk it loosens, which is why it eases. Too much load too quickly has frayed it where it’s anchored.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried you’d have to stop running. You don’t: we’ll adjust the load so the heel can recover and then build you back up.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him active and at work; offer weight support on his terms.
sharedPlan: Education and a realistic timescale of months
Daily calf and plantar-fascia stretching; progressive strengthening
Paracetamol or topical or short oral NSAID if suitable (BNF)
Physiotherapy if persistent; injection or shockwave (HTG200) only selectively
safetyNet: Unable to weight-bear or pinpoint bone pain: urgent review
Hot, swollen or red heel, or fever
Numbness, tingling, night pain; review at about 6 weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: A textbook story. Marks go to excluding a stress fracture and nerve causes, advising load change rather than rest, and handling his wish to keep running and the weight question well.

items.fail: Not considering a stress fracture after a rapid rise in running.
items.why: Focal bony pain and a positive squeeze test need imaging.
items.fix: Ask about the build-up and do the squeeze test.

items.why: The diagnosis is clinical; imaging is for atypical features.
Load modification with tolerable activity is recommended.

items.fail: Injection or shockwave at first presentation.
items.why: Not first-line; injection risks rupture and fat-pad atrophy; HTG200 requires special arrangements.
items.fix: Stretch, strengthen, footwear; physiotherapy if persistent.

items.why: He started running to address it; blame disengages him.
items.fix: Offer support and link it to his own goal.

items.why: Recovery often takes months; false hope reduces adherence.
items.fix: Give an honest timescale and a review date.
